imo-1999-01.title: Centroid, circle, equal arcs
imo-1999-01.body:
**Regular polygons work.** Put the vertices at angles $\frac{2\pi k}{n}$ on a circle centred at the origin. The perpendicular bisector of the vertices $k=i$ and $k=j$ is the line through the centre at angle $\frac{\pi(i+j)}n$; reflection in it sends the angle $\theta$ to $\frac{2\pi(i+j)}n-\theta$, hence the vertex $k$ to the vertex $i+j-k\pmod n$. So it maps the vertex set onto itself.

**Conversely**, let $S$ be a finite set with the property.

*All points lie on a circle.* Let $G$ be the centroid (average) of the points of $S$. A reflection that maps $S$ onto itself is an affine map permuting the points, so it fixes their average $G$. Hence $G$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of every segment $AB$ ($A,B\in S$), i.e. $GA=GB$. So all points of $S$ lie on a circle $\omega$ with centre $G$ (of positive radius, as the points are distinct).

*Consecutive arcs are equal.* List the points of $S$ around $\omega$ as $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_n$ ($n\ge3$, indices mod $n$). Fix $i$ and let $\sigma$ be the reflection in the perpendicular bisector of $P_{i-1}P_{i+1}$. This line passes through $G$, so $\sigma$ maps $\omega$ to itself, fixes the two midpoints of the arcs between $P_{i-1}$ and $P_{i+1}$, and swaps $P_{i-1}$ and $P_{i+1}$; therefore it maps each of the two arcs between $P_{i-1}$ and $P_{i+1}$ onto itself. The open arc containing $P_i$ contains no other point of $S$, and $\sigma(S)=S$, so $\sigma(P_i)=P_i$. Thus $P_i$ is the midpoint of that arc: the arcs $P_{i-1}P_i$ and $P_iP_{i+1}$ are equal.

As this holds for every $i$, all $n$ arcs between consecutive points are equal, and $S$ is the vertex set of a regular $n$-gon.

**Answer:** the sets of vertices of regular polygons. ∎

imo-1999-02.title: Bound $x_i^2+x_j^2$ by $\sum x_k^2$, then AM–GM
imo-1999-02.body:
Write $Q=\sum_kx_k^2$, $P=\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j$, so $\left(\sum x_k\right)^2=Q+2P$.

**The bound with $C=\frac18$.** For each pair, $x_i^2+x_j^2\le Q$ and $x_ix_j\ge0$, so
$$\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j(x_i^2+x_j^2)\le Q\cdot P=\frac12\,Q\cdot2P\le\frac12\left(\frac{Q+2P}{2}\right)^2=\frac18\left(\sum_kx_k\right)^4,$$
by AM–GM ($uv\le\left(\frac{u+v}2\right)^2$).

**$C$ cannot be smaller.** For $x_1=x_2=1$ and the other $x_i=0$, the left side is $1\cdot1\cdot(1+1)=2$ and $\left(\sum x_i\right)^4=16$, so $C\ge\frac2{16}=\frac18$. Hence the least constant is $C=\frac18$.

**Equality.** We need equality in both steps.
- First step: for every pair with $x_ix_j>0$ we need $x_i^2+x_j^2=Q$, i.e. all other $x_k$ are $0$. So if some pair has $x_ix_j>0$, there are exactly two non-zero variables; if three were non-zero, a pair of them would violate this.
- Second step: $Q=2P$.

If at most one variable is non-zero, say $x_1=s$, then $Q=s^2$, $P=0$, and $Q=2P$ forces $s=0$: all variables are $0$ (equality $0=0$). If exactly two are non-zero, $x_i=u$, $x_j=v$, then $Q=2P$ means $u^2+v^2=2uv$, i.e. $u=v$. Conversely, $x_i=x_j=u$, others $0$, gives left side $2u^4$ and right side $\frac18(2u)^4=2u^4$.

**Answer:** $C=\frac18$, with equality exactly when two of the $x_i$ are equal and the rest are zero (including the all-zero case). ∎

imo-1999-02.title: Smoothing
imo-1999-02.body:
Normalise $\sum x_i=1$. Since $\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j(x_i^2+x_j^2)=\sum_ix_i^3\sum_{j\ne i}x_j=\sum_ix_i^3(1-x_i)$, we must maximise $\sum_iF(x_i)$ with $F(x)=x^3-x^4$.

*Merging step.* If $u,v\ge0$ and $u+v\le\frac34$ then $F(u)+F(v)\le F(u+v)+F(0)$: indeed $F(u+v)-F(u)-F(v)=uv\big(3(u+v)-(4u^2+6uv+4v^2)\big)\ge uv\big(3(u+v)-4(u+v)^2\big)\ge0$.

If three of the numbers were positive, two of them would have sum at most $\frac23\cdot1<\frac34$ (the two smallest of three positive numbers with total $\le1$), and we could merge them without decreasing the sum. Repeating, we reduce to at most two non-zero numbers $a+b=1$, where $a^3+b^3=1-3ab$ and $a^4+b^4=(1-2ab)^2-2a^2b^2=1-4ab+2a^2b^2$, so $F(a)+F(b)$ is $ab-2a^2b^2=\frac18-2\left(ab-\frac14\right)^2\le\frac18$, with equality at $ab=\frac14$, i.e. $a=b=\frac12$. This again gives $C=\frac18$. ∎

imo-1999-03.title: Split by colour: an independent set and an explicit cover
imo-1999-03.body:
Let $n=2k$; we show the answer is $k(k+1)=\frac{n(n+2)}4$. Number the rows and columns $1,\ldots,2k$ and colour cell $(i,j)$ **white** if $i+j$ is even and **black** if $i+j$ is odd. Neighbours have opposite colours, so the white cells must be dominated by marked **black** cells and the black cells by marked **white** cells. We show each colour needs exactly $\frac{k(k+1)}2$ marked cells.

**Lower bound.** Two distinct cells have a common neighbour exactly when their taxicab distance $|\Delta i|+|\Delta j|$ is $2$. Consider the anti-diagonals $i+j=s$ with $s\equiv2\pmod4$ (they consist of white cells). On such an anti-diagonal choose the cells with $i$ odd if $s\le2k$, and the cells with $i$ even if $s\ge2k+2$. Call the chosen set $W$.
- Two chosen cells on the same anti-diagonal differ by a multiple of $(2,-2)$: distance $\ge4$.
- Chosen cells on different anti-diagonals have $|\Delta(i+j)|\ge4$: distance $\ge4$.

So no two cells of $W$ share a neighbour, and each needs its own marked black neighbour: at least $|W|$ marked black cells.

*Counting $W$.* For $s\le2k$ the anti-diagonal has cells with $i=1,\ldots,s-1$, of which $\frac s2$ have $i$ odd; with $s=2,6,10,\ldots$ this gives $1,3,5,\ldots$ (all odd numbers $\le k$). For $s\ge2k+2$ the cells have $i=s-2k,\ldots,2k$ (both ends even), giving $2k+1-\frac s2$ chosen cells; as $\frac s2$ runs over the odd numbers in $[k+1,2k-1]$ this gives $2,4,6,\ldots$ (all even numbers $\le k$). So $|W|=1+2+\cdots+k=\frac{k(k+1)}2$.

The reflection $(i,j)\mapsto(i,2k+1-j)$ preserves adjacency and swaps the colours, so it maps $W$ to a set of black cells with the same property, which needs $\frac{k(k+1)}2$ marked white cells. Altogether $N\ge k(k+1)$.

**Construction.** Let $\mathcal B$ be the set of black cells
- $(i,\,i+d)$ with $d\equiv1\pmod4$, $d>0$, $i$ odd (on the diagonals $1,5,9,\ldots$ above the main diagonal, in odd rows), and
- $(j+d,\,j)$ with $d\equiv3\pmod4$, $d>0$, $j$ odd (on the diagonals $3,7,11,\ldots$ below it, in odd columns),

all inside the board. The diagonal $d$ contributes $\frac{2k-d+1}2$ cells, so $|\mathcal B|=k+(k-1)+(k-2)+\cdots+1=\frac{k(k+1)}2$ (above: $k,k-2,\ldots$; below: $k-1,k-3,\ldots$).

*Every white cell $(x,y)$ has a neighbour in $\mathcal B$.* Let $e=y-x$ (even).
- $e\equiv0\pmod4$, $e\ge0$: if $x$ is odd, then $y$ is odd, so $y<2k$ and $(x,y+1)\in\mathcal B$ ($d=e+1$); if $x$ is even, $(x-1,y)\in\mathcal B$ ($d=e+1$).
- $e\equiv2\pmod4$, $e>0$: if $x$ is odd, $(x,y-1)\in\mathcal B$ ($d=e-1$); if $x$ is even, then $x<2k$ (as $y=x+e\le2k$) and $(x+1,y)\in\mathcal B$ ($d=e-1$).
- $e<0$, $f=-e\equiv0\pmod4$: if $y$ is odd, $(x-1,y)\in\mathcal B$ ($d=f-1$); if $y$ is even, then $y<2k$ and $(x,y+1)\in\mathcal B$ ($d=f-1$).
- $e<0$, $f=-e\equiv2\pmod4$: if $y$ is odd, then $x=y+f$ is odd, so $x<2k$ and $(x+1,y)\in\mathcal B$ ($d=f+1$); if $y$ is even, $(x,y-1)\in\mathcal B$ ($d=f+1$).

Mark $\mathcal B$ together with its mirror image under $(i,j)\mapsto(i,2k+1-j)$, which is a set of $\frac{k(k+1)}2$ white cells dominating all black cells. This marks $k(k+1)$ cells and every cell has a marked neighbour. (For $n=4$: black $(1,2),(3,4),(4,1)$ and white $(1,3),(3,1),(4,4)$.)

**Answer:** $N_{\min}=k(k+1)=\dfrac{n(n+2)}4$. ∎

imo-1999-04.title: Smallest prime factor and a binomial expansion
imo-1999-04.body:
$n=1$ works for every prime $p$. Now let $n\ge2$.

**$p=2$.** The condition is $n\mid1^n+1=2$, so $n=2$: the pair $(2,2)$.

**$p$ odd.** Then $(p-1)^n+1$ is odd, so $n$ is odd. Let $q$ be the smallest prime factor of $n$; $q$ is odd and $q\mid(p-1)^n+1$, so $(p-1)^n\equiv-1\pmod q$ and in particular $q\nmid p-1$. Let $r$ be the order of $p-1$ modulo $q$. From $(p-1)^{2n}\equiv1$ and Fermat, $r\mid\gcd(2n,q-1)$. Every prime factor of $n$ is $\ge q$, so $\gcd(n,q-1)=1$ and $\gcd(2n,q-1)\mid2$. So $r\in\{1,2\}$, i.e. $(p-1)^2\equiv1$. If $p-1\equiv1$, then $(p-1)^n\equiv1\not\equiv-1$; hence $p-1\equiv-1\pmod q$, i.e. $q\mid p$, so $q=p$.

Thus $p\mid n$; with $n\le2p$ and $n$ odd this gives $n=p$. We need $p^{p-1}\mid(p-1)^p+1$. By the binomial theorem,
$$(p-1)^p+1=\sum_{i=0}^{p}\binom pi p^i(-1)^{p-i}+1=\big(-1+1\big)+p\cdot p-\binom p2p^2+\cdots=p^2+(\text{multiple of }p^3),$$
because $\binom p2p^2=\frac{p-1}{2}p^3$ and all later terms contain $p^3$. So exactly $p^2$ divides $(p-1)^p+1$, and we need $p-1\le2$, i.e. $p=3$. Indeed $3^2=9\mid2^3+1=9$: the pair $(3,3)$.

**Answer:** $(1,p)$ for all primes $p$, $(2,2)$ and $(3,3)$.

imo-1999-05.title: Homothety and a distance computation
imo-1999-05.body:
Let $\Gamma,\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2$ have centres $O,O_1,O_2$ and radii $R,r_1,r_2$. Use vectors with $O$ as the origin. Internal tangency gives $O_1=\left(1-\frac{r_1}R\right)M$ and $|O_1|=R-r_1$, and similarly $|O_2|=R-r_2$. Also $|O_2-O_1|=r_1$, since $O_2\in\Gamma_1$.

**The homothety.** Let $h(X)=M+\frac{r_1}R(X-M)=O_1+\frac{r_1}RX$, the homothety with centre $M$ and ratio $\frac{r_1}{R}$; it maps $\Gamma$ onto $\Gamma_1$. The point $M$ is not on the radical axis $AB$ (its power is $0$ for $\Gamma_1$ but positive for $\Gamma_2$, since $M\ne N$ lies outside $\Gamma_2$), so $A\ne M$. The line $MA$ meets $\Gamma_1$ at $M$ and at $h(A)\ne M$; hence $C=h(A)$, and likewise $D=h(B)$. So line $CD=h(\text{line }AB)$.

**The radical axis.** Let $u=\frac{O_2-O_1}{r_1}$ (a unit vector). The radical axis is perpendicular to $O_1O_2$, so it has the form $X\cdot u=c$. A point $X$ on it satisfies $|X-O_1|^2-r_1^2=|X-O_2|^2-r_2^2$, i.e.
$$2X\cdot(O_2-O_1)=r_1^2-r_2^2+|O_2|^2-|O_1|^2=(r_1-r_2)(r_1+r_2)+(r_1-r_2)(2R-r_1-r_2)=2R(r_1-r_2).$$
So $c=X\cdot u=\dfrac{R(r_1-r_2)}{r_1}$.

**The line $CD$.** If $X\cdot u=c$, then $h(X)\cdot u=O_1\cdot u+\frac{r_1}{R}c=O_1\cdot u+(r_1-r_2)$. So $CD$ is the line $Y\cdot u=O_1\cdot u+r_1-r_2$, again perpendicular to $u$.

**Distance from $O_2$.** Since $O_2\cdot u-O_1\cdot u=(O_2-O_1)\cdot u=r_1$, the distance from $O_2$ to $CD$ is
$$\big|O_2\cdot u-O_1\cdot u-(r_1-r_2)\big|=|r_1-(r_1-r_2)|=r_2 .$$
The distance from the centre of $\Gamma_2$ to line $CD$ equals its radius, so $CD$ is tangent to $\Gamma_2$. ∎

imo-1999-06.title: Values on the image, then differences of values
imo-1999-06.body:
Let $A=f(\mathbb R)$ be the image and $c=f(0)$. For $a\in A$, pick $y$ with $f(y)=a$; the equation reads
$$f(x-a)=f(a)+xa+f(x)-1\qquad(x\in\mathbb R,\ a\in A). \tag{1}$$

**$f$ on its image.** Put $x=a$ in (1): $c=2f(a)+a^2-1$, so
$$f(a)=\frac{c+1-a^2}{2}\qquad(a\in A). \tag{2}$$

**Every real number is a difference of two values.** $f\equiv0$ is not a solution ($0=-1$), so there is $a_0\in A$ with $a_0\ne0$. By (1), $f(x-a_0)-f(x)=a_0x+f(a_0)-1$. As $x$ runs over $\mathbb R$, the right side takes every real value (it is linear in $x$ with slope $a_0\ne0$), while the left side is a difference of two elements of $A$. So $A-A=\mathbb R$.

**The formula.** Let $z\in\mathbb R$ and write $z=a_1-a_2$ with $a_1,a_2\in A$. By (1) with $x=a_1$, $a=a_2$, and then (2),
$$f(z)=f(a_1-a_2)=f(a_2)+a_1a_2+f(a_1)-1=\frac{c+1-a_2^2}2+a_1a_2+\frac{c+1-a_1^2}2-1=c-\frac{(a_1-a_2)^2}{2}=c-\frac{z^2}{2}.$$
So $f(x)=c-\frac{x^2}2$ for all $x$. Comparing with (2) at any $a\in A$: $c-\frac{a^2}2=\frac{c+1-a^2}2$, so $c=1$.

**Check.** For $f(x)=1-\frac{x^2}2$ and $a=f(y)$: the left side is $1-\frac{(x-a)^2}2$, and the right side is $\left(1-\frac{a^2}2\right)+xa+\left(1-\frac{x^2}2\right)-1=1-\frac{(x-a)^2}{2}$. ✓

**Answer:** $f(x)=1-\dfrac{x^2}{2}$.
